newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin may revise Belarus deal over TV crew row.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin may revise Belarus deal over TV crew row.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday suggested Moscow might revise a union charter with Belarus in a row over the detention of a Russian television crew.

Yeltsin said he was "surprised and indignant" over the arrest by Belarussian authorities of a Russian Public Television (ORT) team on Saturday for what they said was illegally filming and crossing the Belarus-Lithuania border.

Interfax quoted Yeltsin as asking reporters at the Volzhsky Utyos holiday residence in central Russia to convey his words to Belarus hardline President Alexander Lukashenko: "I am indignant over your actions. I want you to explain what is happening."
Yeltsin said he hoped the incident could be settled, but if it was not, then: "Let us reconsider the charter and the agreements which we have signed". He added: "We do not touch Belarus journalists."

In May Lukashenko signed a charter on a loose union between his country of 10 million and 150 million-strong Russia. The deal was watered down by liberals in Moscow who feared it would give the hardline president too much say in Russia's policy.
One of the points in the union charter provided for the protection of press freedoms.

Lukashenko, seen by liberals in Moscow and in the West as increasingly authoritarian, defended the action against ORT journalists on Monday and accused the Russian media of waging an information war against him.
Earlier Lukashenko closed some Belarussian newspapers down and ousted the editors of others. Some opposition newspapers are now published in Lithuania.
The crew, headed ORT bureau chief Pavel Sheremet, were detained late on Saturday and are being held in a KGB prison in the town of Grodno.
Belarus officials said Sheremet's actions were punishable under the former Soviet republic's criminal code, and that he could get up to five years in prison.

Sheremet was accused by the Belarussian authorities of biased reporting earlier this month and stripped of his foreign ministry media accreditation. Earlier this year, Belarus expelled a reporter for Russia's NTV television.

Lukashenko rewrote the constitution in November last year after a landslide win in a referendum which critics said was illegitimate and ignored the old constitution. The new basic law gives him vast powers.
